content.overview: Coolant wear moves heat off the body: passive phase-change vests absorb heat as wax melts, and active liquid garments pump cooled water through tubes, a technology NASA has flown since Apollo. Standard grade: real PCM and pumped-loop cooling with honest duration math.
details: Humans shed about 100 W at rest and 300-500 W in heavy work; cooling must match metabolic heat.
Latent heat is the trick: melting 1 kg of PCM at 180 kJ/kg absorbs the same heat as warming 43 kg of water by 1 C.
Cooling time is roughly stored latent heat divided by heat load: a 1 kg PCM vest at 200 W lasts about 15 minutes per 180 kJ.
Liquid garments win on duration: a pumped loop rejects heat continuously as long as the chiller runs.

details: Size the heat load first: rest, work, and environment set the watts the garment must move.
For passive cooling, place PCM packs over the torso's high-blood-flow zones; 0.5-1.5 kg is the wearable range.
For active cooling, route small-bore tubing in a dense serpentine and pair with a compact pump and heat exchanger.
Seal all liquid paths and test at 1.5x working pressure; a leak inside protective gear is a mission failure.
Add a simple controller: skin-temperature feedback beats fixed cooling for comfort and duration.
